Urgent hiring for Senior AI Infrastructure Engineer (W2/1099)

Job Title: Senior AI Infrastructure Engineer / HPC – GPU Cluster & Fabric
Location: Plano, TX
Long term contract
Only W2/1099

About the role
You own everything beneath the operating system: GPU node architecture, the compute and storage fabrics, bare-metal provisioning, high-performance storage design, and the facility constraints that decide whether an AI factory is buildable. This is the role that makes clusters scale linearly instead of falling over at sixteen nodes — and the role customers rely on when their training job stops scaling and nobody knows why.

What you’ll do
Design GPU cluster physical and logical topology: node configuration, rail-optimized fabric layout, oversubscription ratios, failure domains.
Architect and deploy InfiniBand (NDR/XDR) and high-performance Ethernet fabrics — subnet management and UFM, adaptive routing, congestion control, SHARP offload.
Own high-performance storage architecture for AI: parallel filesystems (WEKA, Luster, GPFS, VAST, DDN), GPU Direct Storage, NVMe-oF and NFS-over-RDMA, and sizing for data loader read, checkpoint burst writes, and artifact serving.
Own bare-metal lifecycle — cluster provisioning (Bright Cluster Manager or equivalent), firmware and driver baselines, imaging, node validation and burn-in.
Produce BOMs and sizing for compute, network, optics, and storage; validate against customer power, cooling, floor loading, and lead times.
Run scaling and fabric benchmarks (NCCL bus bandwidth, IB performance tests, IOR/fio) and own cluster acceptance criteria.
Diagnose interconnect and scaling faults: link errors, topology binding, NUMA and PCIe affinity, GPU Direct RDMA verification, I/O stalls.
Set infrastructure standards for the offshore delivery pod and review their work before customer delivery.

What you need
6+ years HPC or AI infrastructure engineering; production multi-node GPU cluster experience is mandatory.
Deep InfiniBand and/or high-performance Ethernet: fabric design, subnet management, congestion behavior, and troubleshooting at scale.
NVIDIA GPU platforms — HGX or DGX-class systems, driver and firmware stack.
Parallel or scale-out filesystem design and performance tuning for I/O-intensive workloads.
Bare-metal cluster provisioning and deep Linux systems engineering.
Data center fundamentals: rack power, airflow, direct-liquid cooling concepts, cabling and optics planning.

Setter goes further.

Hiring changes, filings, company developments, contract changes and the things happening inside an account that you won’t necessarily find in a standard intent feed.

Then we waterfall-enrich the contact data to give the SDR the best possible route in.

Right company. Right person. Right signal. Then let a great SDR do what they do best.

That’s Setter. 👇

It was a pleasure to welcome the team from FinancialCareers to join us this week at LHH's latest Connections to Jobs event.  The team shared a comprehensive view of the current hiring market, based on the activity of their jobs platform which contains tens of thousands of roles in the FS and Tech sectors, globally.

The outlook is cautiously optimistic. Opportunities are growing in several areas, but success continues to favour those who combine specialist expertise with adaptability, curiosity and a clear understanding of the value they bring.

My top 5 takeaways:

🔹 The market is recovering, but employers remain highly selective. Hiring activity is improving, but candidates need to demonstrate clear impact, relevance and adaptability. 

🔹 Not all sectors are experiencing the same demand. Asset Management, Private Equity, Hedge Funds, Risk, Compliance, Legal Tech and AI-related roles continue to attract investment and hiring activity. 

🔹 Contracting is becoming a strategic route into organisations. Interim and contract hiring remains strong across technology, data, AI, finance and transformation functions. 

🔹 AI is now part of the conversation. From governance and responsible AI to prompt engineering and business applications, employers increasingly expect candidates to have a point of view on AI. 

🔹 Human skills remain the differentiator. Despite widespread AI adoption, critical thinking, judgement, communication and decision-making continue to separate strong candidates from the crowd. 

What hiring trends are you noticing and how is it influencing your job search?

Thank you to Peter Healey, CEO, Rainy Gill VP Marketing and Francois Trepanier, Senior Talent Acquisition for an engaging and insight-rich discussion, and to everyone who joined us from the LHH community.

The Cost —

Recently, I was asked to contract with a company to do ethics training for their AI model. And I wrestled with that. Not because I don’t believe in technology. I do. But training AI can ultimately remove the need for the very people who helped train it.

My ethics stress test keeps pushing the question further. Why are we building this, and why so fast? Who benefits? Who is harmed?

When I push it all the way to the end, I find myself in the same place: Capital. Money. Power. Control.

That is the sacred cow.

However history has shown us that when capital becomes the motivator, people become casualties.

But we’re not numbers, headcount, or labor costs. We’re human beings. Mothers, fathers, spouses, friends, neighbors. People with dreams and lives beyond the walls of a company. People who have said, “I’m not just trading my time for pay. This is my life.”

That’s what we have to wrestle with. When we reduce people to what they cost, we forget what they contribute. We forget the person sitting across from us has a life. A family. A story. A dream. Maybe that dream has already cost them something.

Look at Walmart’s real-time pricing technology. Amazon’s abandoned recruiting AI learned from historical hiring patterns and reproduced disadvantages for women. At Oracle, employees have reportedly been laid off after helping train AI systems that could replace portions of their work.

These aren’t just technology stories. They’re human stories.
That’s where ethics begins.

What happens when a company researches a moral question and finds something it didn’t want to find? What happens when the ethical answer costs more? What happens when going backward is right, but costs money? Who helps a company process that—and who tells the truth?

Ethics can’t be something we study until the answer makes us uncomfortable, then put the research back on the shelf. Sometimes the answer requires us to slow down or admit: We got this wrong.

Maybe that’s wisdom.

Here’s the other side of the cost.

We were never designed to give a company most of our life. Long before AI, that arrangement already had a cost. How many dreams have been put on hold? The business idea. The invention. The book. The art. The parent who wanted to be home with their kids. The person who knew there was more in them but was too exhausted to reach for it.

That exhaustion is a cost too. We stopped noticing it because we normalized it.

If AI is disrupting your work, hear this:

This doesn’t have to be your ending.

Maybe you spent years doing something you never dreamed of—only to become a line item.

Create something. Try something. Dream again. Find your art. Hope again.

Maybe this disruption becomes an invitation to build what you never had the time or energy to build before.

Because technology may change the work.

But it doesn’t have to determine the worth of the worker.
